title: Share what a story makes you think and feel
intro: I can notice a story moment, share my response and listen to a different response. There is no one feeling that every reader must have.
exampleTitle: One event can lead to different responses
example: In the supplied story, Niko’s boot goes missing in the rain and a neighbour returns it. One reader says, “I felt worried when the boot was missing.” Another says, “I felt pleased when the neighbour helped.” Each response connects with an actual event. Neither reader has to copy the other’s feeling.
steps: Find the moment you are responding to
First say who is involved and what happens. Then share your thought or feeling. Keeping those parts separate helps a listener understand your response.
Niko’s boot is missing. Later, the neighbour returns it.
Which moment could connect with feeling relieved?
The boot being returned could bring relief. Other feelings are welcome when the reader explains their connection with a real story moment.
Show a response in words or a drawing
You can say, draw, sign or begin to write your response. Point out which part represents the story and which part shows what you think or feel. An adult can write your own words for you.
Another short story: Jo has one pear. Jo gives the pear to a hungry friend.
What might you think about Jo’s action?

For example, “I think Jo is generous because Jo gives food to the hungry friend.” Generous means willing to share. Other supported thoughts are possible; the action is the clue, not a rule about what Jo always does.
Make a connection without changing the story

A story may remind you of an experience. Say what is similar and what is different. You may use an imagined situation or pass on a private memory. Your experience does not prove an unstated story fact.
Story: Niko loses a boot. Possible connection: a pretend missing toy that is later found.
Could a lost toy be a useful connection even though it is not a boot?
Yes. Losing and finding something can be the connection. Keep the objects distinct: the story has a boot; the imagined example has a toy.
mistakes: “The character and I must feel the same.”
Your response can differ. Name the event and explain your own response.
“A neat drawing is the goal.”
The drawing helps communicate a response; drawing skill is not the literature skill.
“One action proves everything about a character.”
Use the action to support a careful thought about this moment.
activity: Hear the Niko story. Choose one moment. Draw, say or show a response and identify the clue. Listen to a partner’s different response and repeat the moment they chose.
adjust: Starter: point to the missing or returned boot moment. Core: share a response with its clue. Stretch: compare two supported responses to the same moment.
safety: Adult: read and model when needed. Accept speech, sign, AAC, pointing or a drawing with explanation. Use short turns. A page answer does not prove an actual conversation, reading performance or physical action.
tricky: A puppy finds its lost owner. “I felt relieved when they met again.” Does this connect feeling and event?
Yes. It names the reader’s feeling and the reunion that prompted it. A different supported feeling can also fit.
A bear loses a hat. Must every reader feel sad?
No. A reader might be worried, curious or feel something else. Ask what in the story prompted the response.
A character keeps trying after falling in a pretend climbing story. Can I think they are determined?
Yes. Continuing to try supports that thought. It does not show that real unsafe climbing should be copied.
faq: Does a child have to tell a private experience?
No. Use an imagined connection, another text or a simple response to the event.
Does the response need the word because?
No. A spoken explanation, pointing with a clear message or an adult-scribed sentence can show the link.

title: Meet story characters and find what happens
intro: I can recognise a story, fairytale or story poem, find who takes part and locate its beginning and ending.
exampleTitle: A poem can tell events too
example: The supplied bird poem uses separate lines and tells connected events. The bird wakes, stretches, flies and lands. The bird is the character; waking and landing are events. The beginning introduces the waking bird and the ending brings it to the tree. Lines and rhythm do not stop a poem from telling a story.
steps: Notice the kind of literary text

Listen to the supplied Mina story and bird poem. One is written as story sentences; the other is arranged in lines. Both can have characters and connected events. These are useful clues, not rules for every poem.
Mina finds a shell, takes it home, listens and returns it to the beach. The bird poem has four lines.
Can both examples have characters and events?
Yes. Mina and the bird are characters. Finding a shell and flying are events. A poem may tell a story; some other poems describe an idea without a story sequence.
Separate who from what happened
A character takes part in the text. An event is something that happens. Ask who for a character and what happened for an event. A place or object is not automatically a character.
Cards: Mina / returns the shell / beach.
Which card names a character, and which names an event?
Mina names the character. Returns the shell names an event. Beach names a place. In another imagined story a place or object might act as a character, so use the actual text.
Find the beginning and ending in the text

Read from the first story event to the final one. A cover or title is usually not a story event. Notice a familiar opening or a magical event when comparing fairytales. Not every fairytale needs a princess or a moral.
Original fairytale miniature: “Once upon a time, a fox found a key. The key opened a cloud door. At last the fox locked the door and went home.”
What begins and ends this miniature, and which event is magical?
It begins with the fox finding a key and ends with the fox going home after locking the door. A key opening a cloud door is the imagined magical event.
mistakes: “Every poem is only a rhyme.”
Some poems tell events and some do not rhyme. Inspect the actual text.
“Mina and returning are both characters.”
Mina is who; returning the shell is what happens.
“Every story begins once upon a time.”
Some do; others introduce a character, place or event in different words.
activity: Read the two supplied complete texts. Use cards marked Character, Beginning and Ending to identify the evidence. Compare the magical fox miniature. For the First Nations book activity in the elaborations, prepare the named actual book first.
adjust: Starter: choose between Mina and an event. Core: identify a character plus first and final event. Stretch: compare how the story and poem begin and end.
safety: Adult: read and model when needed. Accept speech, sign, AAC, pointing or a drawing with explanation. Use short turns. A page answer does not prove an actual conversation, reading performance or physical action.
tricky: Is the printed title always the first story event?
No. Look at what happens when the text itself begins. A title can give clues without being an event.
Must a fairytale have a princess?
No. The magical fox miniature has no princess. Use features present in that text rather than a compulsory checklist.
The bird poem ends at a tree. Can we say the bird builds a nest next?
That might be a new prediction, but building a nest is not an event stated in this poem.
faq: Must children independently decode these texts?
No. An adult may read them aloud; this lesson concerns literary features.
Can one book stand for all First Nations storytelling?
No. Name its creators and describe only features actually found in that particular work.

title: Listen, echo and play with literary sounds
intro: I can hear and copy a rhythm or repeated sound in a short poem, rhyme or chant. I can join in in a comfortable way.
exampleTitle: Keep a steady pulse; notice the words’ rhythm
example: An adult can say the supplied original rhyme slowly while tapping four even beats per line. The beat is the steady pulse; the spoken rhythm includes longer and shorter sounds and pauses. Three and me rhyme by sound. Copy a small part first, then join the two lines. A printed pattern is a reminder for an adult model, not recorded audio.
steps: Listen and echo a small pattern

An adult models “Red bird, blue bird, hop-hop-stop.” Listen to the whole unit, then echo its words, timing and pause. Begin slowly and repeat the same unit. A comfortable tap, sway or AAC rhythm control can accompany the model.
Original chant: “Red bird, blue bird, hop-hop-stop. Red bird, blue bird, hop-hop-stop.”
Which words repeat as the whole unit?
Red bird, blue bird, hop-hop-stop repeats. The learner can hear the adult’s model and echo it; identifying the printed unit alone does not establish a rhythm performance.
Hear rhyme and repeated sounds
Rhyme concerns the spoken ending; repeated beginning sounds are another sound pattern. Say the words aloud. Letter appearance alone cannot settle whether they rhyme.
Say moon, spoon, fish. Then say “Busy bees buzz.”
Which two words rhyme, and which beginning sound repeats in the phrase?
Moon and spoon rhyme. The /b/ sound repeats in busy, bees and buzz. The spoken sound is the clue.
Join words with an agreed action or pause

Choose actions that help you follow the model, rather than race. Compare a steady pulse with a pattern that includes a pause. Adapt movement to the learner. There is no need to stand, stamp or clap loudly.
Adult models clap, clap, pause; clap, clap, pause. The pause lasts one agreed pulse.
What needs to stay in place when you copy it?
The two claps and the pause, in that order and timing. Use quiet taps or another comfortable signal. Removing the pause changes this pattern.
mistakes: “Rhythm and rhyme are the same.”
Rhyme is a matching ending sound; rhythm is how sounds and pauses move through time.
“Going faster makes it better.”
Keep the modelled order and pace first.
“Matching spelling proves a rhyme.”
Listen to the endings. Blue and you can rhyme despite different spellings.
activity: An adult models the original rhyme and chant. Echo a short part, then join a full repetition. Try a new quiet action while keeping the same words and timing. Use the separately prepared named poem activity to explore one First Nations poet’s work.
adjust: Starter: echo two or three words. Core: copy a complete short unit with its pause. Stretch: offer a new line ending with a fitting rhyming word and try it against the same modelled pace.
safety: Adult: read and model when needed. Accept speech, sign, AAC, pointing or a drawing with explanation. Use short turns. A page answer does not prove an actual conversation, reading performance or physical action.
tricky: Do blue and you need the same spelling to rhyme?
No. Their spoken ending sounds match.
If I say the right words but miss the agreed pause, have I copied the whole pattern?
Not yet. The pause is part of this model. Slow down and echo it again.
Can I hear a rhythm in a poem without rhyming words?
Yes. Rhythm can come from timing, repeated phrases and stressed sounds without matching line endings.
faq: Does the page play a recording?
No. An adult supplies the live spoken model. Reading a transcript is different from hearing or performing its rhythm.
Must every child use the same body movement?
No. Choose an accessible way to join in, and observe the intended sound or timing rather than a particular movement.

title: Retell a story and make a new version
intro: I can show the important events in order, then change a clear part to make an adaptation.
exampleTitle: Keep the story anchors when changing an ending
example: In the complete Tama story, Tama plants a seed, waters the growing shoot and sees a yellow flower open. The three actual event drawings support a retell. A new version keeps planting and watering but changes the flower to a tall bean vine. Name the change so a listener can recognise both versions. Any climbing scene is pretend play, not a real climbing task.
steps: Choose and order important events
Read or hear the whole short story first. Select events needed to follow it. Check first, next and finally against the story, not the colours or sizes of the cards.
Tama plants a seed. Tama waters the shoot each day. A yellow flower opens.
Which event must begin this retell?
Planting the seed. Watering the growing shoot follows; the flower opening is the ending. This is the order stated in the story.
Show the same event in another way
A drawing, puppet scene, oral retell or freeze-frame can represent an event. Tell your listener who is present and what happens. The medium can change while the important event stays the same.
Choose “Tama waters the shoot” from the supplied sequence.
How could you show that event without writing a long paragraph?
Draw Tama watering, use a puppet with a pretend watering can, or say the event. Explain which story moment you mean. Drawing quality and handwriting are not the retelling goal.
Adapt one part and check the new sequence

Keep enough familiar parts to recognise the source. Change one character, place, event or ending, then check that the rest still follows. Creative changes are welcome; the new version must remain understandable.
Keep Tama planting and watering. Replace the yellow flower ending with a tall bean vine.
What stayed the same and what changed?
Tama’s planting and care stay. The plant at the ending changes. Explain any new event as part of your adaptation rather than claiming it was in the original.
mistakes: “A retell needs every tiny detail.”
Choose the main connected events.
“I can order the cards by colour.”
Use what happened before and after.
“An adaptation has to copy every word.”
Keep recognisable anchors and make a deliberate change.
activity: Hear the Tama story. Use the three supplied drawings to retell it. Draw a new ending or act it with safe pretend materials. A partner says what stayed the same and what changed.
adjust: Starter: fix the first and last cards and place the middle. Core: retell all three events. Stretch: change one part and explain how the new ending still connects.
safety: Adult: read and model when needed. Accept speech, sign, AAC, pointing or a drawing with explanation. Use short turns. A page answer does not prove an actual conversation, reading performance or physical action.
tricky: Is naming seed, water, flower a connected retell by itself?
It names useful objects. Add what happens: Tama plants the seed, waters the shoot and sees the flower open.
If I change every character, event and place, will a listener recognise this adaptation?
They may not. Keep some clear anchors and explain the intended link.
Does clicking an event picture show that I performed the story?
No. A choice can show recognition. An adult would need to observe the actual retell or performance separately.
faq: Must a child write to retell?
No. Speech, sign, pictures, AAC, puppets and supported performance can communicate the sequence.
Can an adaptation have a different ending?
Yes. Make the change clear and check that the new events fit together.

title: Find a familiar text and its job
intro: I can recognise a story, information text, sign or instruction and explain what it helps a reader do.
exampleTitle: The same topic can have different purposes
example: The supplied farm covers and inside texts share an animal topic. Hen’s Hat tells invented events about a hen finding a hat; Farm Facts gives checkable information. Both belong in a farm-animal group, while their main jobs differ. Cover clues support an early prediction; the inside content helps check it.
steps: Use the actual message to name a text
Notice what the text communicates. Characters and connected invented events can suggest a story; facts can suggest information. Pictures appear in both. A text may have more than one purpose.
Hen’s Hat: “Hen found a hat. She wore it to visit Cow.” Farm Facts: “Hens are birds. They lay eggs.”
Which text is mainly giving information?
Farm Facts gives checkable facts about hens. Hen’s Hat tells invented events. The pictures alone do not establish those jobs.
Explain an everyday symbol’s purpose

A symbol can guide or give a familiar shared message quickly. Look at the shown features and their context. An adult should explain unfamiliar symbols; a classroom drawing is not a replacement for official safety instruction.
The original green exit example shows an arrow, doorway and moving figure beside EXIT.
What does it help people find?
An exit route. The arrow shows direction and the doorway connects with leaving. Real buildings have their own actual signs and safety directions.
Choose and group texts for a purpose
First ask what you need. Then choose a text whose actual content can help. Topic tells what it is about; purpose tells its job. Two texts on one topic can do different jobs.
Task: find facts about hens. Choices: Hen’s Hat / Farm Facts / two numbered steps for folding paper.
Which helps with this task, and which two belong in a farm-animal topic group?
Farm Facts helps find hen facts. Hen’s Hat and Farm Facts share the farm-animal topic. The folding instructions have a different topic and guide an action.
mistakes: “A cover picture proves the purpose.”
Check the title and inside content too.
“Information cannot be enjoyable.”
Facts can be interesting and entertaining. Identify the main job with evidence.
“Same topic means same type.”
Compare what the texts actually do with that topic.
activity: Use the supplied cover-and-content pair, exit example and paper instructions. Name each type and its useful job. Put the two farm texts together, then explain their different purposes.
adjust: Starter: match a text with one clear purpose. Core: explain a clue. Stretch: group by topic first, then compare purpose within the group.
safety: Adult: read and model when needed. Accept speech, sign, AAC, pointing or a drawing with explanation. Use short turns. A page answer does not prove an actual conversation, reading performance or physical action.
tricky: Would any frog story answer a question about what frogs eat?
Not necessarily. Choose a reliable information text that actually supplies the needed fact.
Can a drawing be in an information text?
Yes. A labelled drawing can explain real information.
Is a school crossing sign mainly a story?
No. It guides or warns road users about a crossing. Discuss the actual local sign with an adult; this page is not road-safety training.
faq: Does purpose mean the title?
No. A title may give a clue. Purpose is what the text was made to communicate or help someone do.
Do we have to use only one purpose word?
No. Accept a supported explanation when a text combines jobs, while identifying its main purpose in this example.

title: Listen, take a turn and choose a clear voice
intro: I can listen to another person, respond to their message and use a comfortable volume for the listeners.
exampleTitle: An answer can show that you listened
example: Ari says, “My seed has two leaves.” Mia waits, then asks, “Are the leaves big or small?” Mia’s question connects with the leaves Ari mentioned. A quiet body or eye contact alone would not show that Mia understood. Listening can be shown in several comfortable ways.
steps: Hear the message before adding your idea

Give the speaker time to finish, then recall a detail or ask a connected question. Agree on an accessible turn signal. Movement, AAC and comfortable attention do not make a listener less able to understand.
Ari: “My seed has two leaves.” Possible replies: “How big are the leaves?” / “My lunch is cold.”
Which reply connects with Ari’s idea?
How big are the leaves? It builds on the stated leaves. The lunch reply changes the topic.
Adjust volume for the real listeners

Name who needs to hear you and how far away they are. Speak clearly at a comfortable volume and ask whether they can hear. Outdoors does not always mean shouting, and a bigger audience does not mean straining your voice.
Say “Our plant has grown” to a nearby partner, then to a small group a little farther away.
What should guide the change?
Whether the intended listeners can hear comfortably. Adjust distance or volume as needed. There is no one loudness level that fits every room or person.
Use listening in play and structured tasks
In a pretend shop, respond to the customer’s actual request. In an instruction task, hear the whole short direction before acting. Ask for a repeat if needed. These are different reasons to listen.
Adult says: “Pick up the blue card, then put it beside the book.” Use a safe blue card and a book.
What happens first and next?
First pick up the blue card. Next put it beside the book. Repeating the direction shows recall; observe the action separately if checking that it was carried out.
mistakes: “Still hands prove listening.”
Ask for a relevant response or detail; do not require one body position.
“The loudest voice is best.”
Choose a comfortable volume that reaches these listeners.
“Any reply continues the topic.”
Use a detail from the message when responding.
activity: Use one pretend-shop exchange and one plant discussion. Partners take turns, repeat a detail and add a connected response. Try the blue-card instruction, with repeat or chunking support when needed.
adjust: Starter: use one short message and two reply choices. Core: exchange a relevant turn. Stretch: ask for clarification or adjust the message when a listener cannot hear.
safety: Adult: read and model when needed. Accept speech, sign, AAC, pointing or a drawing with explanation. Use short turns. A page answer does not prove an actual conversation, reading performance or physical action.
tricky: A child looks away but accurately recalls the message. Must we say they were not listening?
No. Eye contact is not compulsory evidence. Consider the actual understanding shown and cultural or access needs.
Is shouting always needed for an outdoor partner?
No. Distance, surrounding sound and listener comfort matter. Move closer or adjust gently.
If I do not understand an instruction, should I guess silently?
Ask for a repeat or explanation, or use an agreed signal. Then check what to do.
faq: Is choosing a reply the same as a live conversation?
No. It is useful preparation. Observe the real exchange separately.
Can AAC count as an interaction turn?
Yes. Provide enough time and an agreed accessible way to listen, contribute and respond.

title: Compare imagined events and real information
intro: I can compare an imaginative text and an information text using their words, pictures and purpose.
exampleTitle: Pictures can support two different text jobs
example: The supplied imaginative frog scene shows a crowned frog inviting the moon to tea. The information diagram shows labelled frog life stages. The story drawing develops an invented event; the diagram helps explain real information. Both are drawings, so the drawing style cannot decide the text type.
steps: Look for what the text is doing
An imaginative text creates events or ideas. An information text mainly explains a real topic with checkable information. Stories can include realistic details, and information can be enjoyable.
Story: “The frog king invited the moon to tea.” Information: “Frogs hatch from eggs.”
Which statement gives checkable real-world information?
Frogs hatch from eggs. The frog king inviting the moon is an invented event. A story need not contain magic to be imaginative.
Choose information that answers your task
Read the question before choosing a text. A relevant heading, label or fact can lead to the answer. A text about the right animal still needs to contain the needed information.
Question: What do many tadpoles eat? Supplied fact: “Many tadpoles eat algae and other plant material; diets vary.”
Which text helps, and what answer does it supply?
The supplied frog information helps. It says many tadpoles eat algae and other plant material, while noting that diets vary. Do not turn many into every.
Compare the jobs of the pictures
Use the words with each picture. A story image can show a character or event; an information diagram can label stages or parts. Neither photographs nor drawings guarantee a purpose by themselves.
Compare the crowned-frog scene and labelled life-cycle diagram supplied here.
How does each image help its text?
The crowned frog develops the imagined story event. The labelled stages help explain a frog’s development. The surrounding text and purpose make the difference clear.
mistakes: “Realistic stories are information texts.”
A story can invent an ordinary event. Look at what the whole text does.
“All drawings are imaginative texts.”
Diagrams can explain checkable information.
“One real object makes a text factual.”
A real frog can appear in invented events.
activity: Read the supplied frog examples. Identify one invented event and one stated fact. Explain what each picture adds. Make an original sentence for each purpose and keep the fact checkable.
adjust: Starter: point to a fact or invented event. Core: compare word and picture clues. Stretch: explain how a realistic story could still be imaginative.
safety: Adult: read and model when needed. Accept speech, sign, AAC, pointing or a drawing with explanation. Use short turns. A page answer does not prove an actual conversation, reading performance or physical action.
tricky: Does a talking fox in boots suggest imagination?
Yes, in that story those character actions are invented. It is a useful clue together with the surrounding text.
A book gives koala facts with labelled photos. What is its likely main purpose?
To inform. Check its actual content; photographs alone are not proof.
Must an information page be boring?
No. Enjoyment does not decide the category. The page can be interesting while explaining facts.
faq: Can a story teach something real?
Yes. Purposes can overlap. Explain what is mainly happening in the particular text.
Should children memorise photograph equals fact?
No. Use the words, labels, image job and overall purpose together.

title: Read the letters, then check the message
intro: I can use taught letter sounds and familiar words to read, reread and ask for help when something does not fit.
example: The supplied microtext reads “Sam sat. / A cat ran.” Read left to right, blend taught sounds and sweep back for the second line. In sat, /s/ /a/ /t/ blend to sat. The word is not sun: the middle and final letters differ. Reread the complete sentence to check meaning after looking through the word.
steps: Track the print and blend taught sounds
Begin at the first word and match one spoken word to each written word. Move back to the start of the next line. Stretch continuous sounds without adding an extra uh; model stop sounds briefly.
Microtext: “Sam sat.” on line one; “A cat ran.” on line two.
After sat, where does the next line begin?
At A on the left of line two. Blend the taught sounds in cat and ran in order. The capital names/letters and the word A need prior teaching or adult support.
Read words you can work through and words you know

A text is decodable for a learner when its sound–letter patterns have been taught. Recognise and verify familiar high-frequency words too. An adult may support untaught parts of an authentic note. Do not substitute a plausible word for the printed one.
Printed target: mat. Compare map. Adult-supported real-life-style note: “Please bring a hat.”
What tells you that mat is not map?
The final letter t represents /t/, while p represents /p/. Look through every letter. In the note, an adult can support Please and bring if their patterns have not been taught.
Pause, repair and reread
If the reading does not match print, grammar or meaning, pause. Look again, blend and reread; ask for help when needed. Context is a check, not permission to guess from the picture or first letter.
Printed sentence: “A fox hid in a den.” The adult deliberately says din for den.
What should you check before rereading?
Check the middle letter e and its taught short sound, then blend den. Reread the whole sentence. A den is a place an animal can shelter; the meaning helps confirm the decoded word.
mistakes: “A picture can replace the letters.”
Use all printed letters first. Pictures may help check meaning.
“Stopping means I failed.”
Pausing to repair or ask is part of reading.
“Any word that makes sense is the printed word.”
A word must also match the actual letters and taught sound patterns.
activity: Use the two-line microtext. Point once for each word, blend an unfamiliar taught word and reread the sentence. Ask an adult to model an untaught pattern. Use the note for supported authentic reading.
adjust: Starter: blend one CVC word with a model. Core: read and reread the short text. Stretch: identify a deliberate close-word misread and explain the letter evidence.
safety: Adult: read and model when needed. Accept speech, sign, AAC, pointing or a drawing with explanation. Use short turns. A page answer does not prove an actual conversation, reading performance or physical action.
tricky: Would seeing a cat picture prove that the printed word is cat?
No. Read the actual letters. A cat picture could accompany a different sentence.
You blend /m/ /a/ /p/. What word do you read?
Map, with the short vowel sound represented by a. The final /p/ matters.
You read “The cat sun” for “The cat sat.” What could you do?
Pause, compare the printed a and t with what you said, blend sat, then reread. Ask for help if the mismatch remains.
faq: Must every Foundation child read this same text independently?
No. Match the text to taught phonics and prior word knowledge. Adult support is appropriate for untaught parts.
Can comprehension support be separated from decoding?
Yes. An adult can read richer authentic texts aloud for comprehension while the child practises reading appropriately decodable print.

title: Use clues to understand and discuss a text
intro: I can predict, make a mind picture, ask a question and retell important ideas. I can change my thinking when new clues appear.
example: The supplied original cover is called The Missing Boot and shows a boot beside muddy pawprints. A dog moving the other boot is one possible prediction, not a proved fact. In the complete miniature, a child is carrying the missing boot to clean it. The new evidence changes the prediction. The muddy prints were a clue with more than one possible explanation.
steps: Predict or visualise from actual clues

Use the title, picture or words to say what might happen. A mind picture can help make sense of a description; you may describe it or show it with gesture rather than seeing a clear inner image. You do not have to close your eyes.
Original sentence: “A small tent stood under a tall tree. A leaf lay beside the tent.”
What could you describe or draw from these words?
A small tent under a tall tree, with a leaf beside it. Colour or weather is not stated. Keep added imagination separate from given details.
Retell the important ideas or facts
Use the main sequence for a story. After information, tell one or two useful facts instead of inventing a story. A summary is brief and keeps the central meaning.
Listen: “Mia carried a blue basket to the gate. A puppy followed her. She put the basket on a bench.” Purpose question: What was Mia carrying?
What was she carrying, and what words support it?
A blue basket. The first sentence supplies both colour and object. Listening to this supplied passage is required; the answer is not guessed from an absent picture.
Ask, connect and revise

Ask a question that helps you understand what is missing. A connection can be to an experience, another text or an imagined situation. It does not prove a hidden fact. Change a prediction when stronger evidence appears.
The Missing Boot ending says a child carries the boot to clean it. Earlier you predicted the dog moved it.
How should you respond to the ending?
Update the prediction: the child is carrying it in this text. You can ask how it got muddy or connect with cleaning something, without inventing an unstated answer.
mistakes: “Any guess is a supported prediction.”
Identify a relevant actual clue. Several predictions may fit.
“A summary repeats every detail.”
Keep the main event or useful facts.
“My memory proves the story happened that way.”
Separate your connection from what this text actually says.
activity: Before reading, use the actual boot cover for a prediction. During reading, describe a mind picture and ask a relevant question. After the complete miniature, revise the prediction and summarise the main event. Prepare the named actual book before its First Nations retell extension.
adjust: Starter: choose a prediction that connects with a visible clue. Core: explain and revise it after reading. Stretch: distinguish a stated detail, a prediction and an unanswered question.
safety: Adult: read and model when needed. Accept speech, sign, AAC, pointing or a drawing with explanation. Use short turns. A page answer does not prove an actual conversation, reading performance or physical action.
tricky: The supplied cover shows clouds and a child with an umbrella. Must it rain next?
Rain is a reasonable possibility, not certain. Check what the text later says.
“The puppy ran to the gate when Dad came home.” What is the key event?
The puppy runs to the gate as Dad arrives. Do not add an unstated reunion scene.
The information sentence says penguins have feathers and cannot fly. Can I report that they have feathers?
Yes. That is a supplied fact. A summary should not add an unsupported claim such as every penguin living in snow.
faq: Does every child need to see a mental picture?
No. A verbal description, gesture or supported drawing can communicate understanding.
Can a prediction be useful even when the ending differs?
Yes. Explain the original clue, then update the idea honestly.

title: Write a short message and edit it together
intro: I can say an idea, record it with words or pictures, read it back and help improve its meaning, capitals, full stops or CVC spelling.
exampleTitle: An edit makes a chosen improvement
example: The supplied draft says “the cat sat”. The intended idea is a cat sitting. Shared editing changes the first letter to T and adds a full stop: “The cat sat.” Read the result back. Cat can be spelt by mapping /k/ /a/ /t/ to c, a, t. The two sentence-boundary edits and the sound-spelling check have different jobs.
steps: Start with a message worth recording

Say or show one idea about a real, imagined or text event. An adult can scribe it while you contribute known words and taught sound–letter choices. A drawing and words should communicate the same intended idea.
Intended message: “My cat sat.” Cat is the CVC target.
Which three sound positions can help spell cat?
/k/ /a/ /t/. Use c, a, t in this word, then blend and reread. My needs prior word knowledge or adult support; do not pretend every word is CVC.
Read your own draft back to a partner

Read or explain what your marks mean to an experienced writer. Compare that intention with the visible draft. You can keep an effective word and change one confusing part. Editing is more than copying neatly.
Draft word cards: “sam the cat fed”. Intended meaning: Sam gave food to the cat.
How could shared editing make that intended event clear?
Arrange the words as “Sam fed the cat.” Capitalise Sam and add the full stop. Keep the intended meaning rather than accepting any different plausible event.
Check one sentence feature at a time
After checking meaning, locate the beginning and ending of each sentence. Find the sentence-opening capital, then the full stop. Check a taught CVC spelling by sounds. One capital may do two jobs.
Complete text: “Sam fed the cat. It sat.”
Which capitals begin sentences, and does Sam need a separate second capital for the name?
S and I begin the two sentences. The same S starts the name Sam and sentence one; no extra capital is needed. The two full stops mark the telling sentences’ endings.
mistakes: “Editing means every word was wrong.”
Keep useful parts and make a chosen improvement.
“Neat copying fixes meaning.”
Read the whole message and compare it with the intended idea.
“Every word here is CVC.”
Cat and sat fit that pattern. Other words need their own taught knowledge or support.
activity: Choose an event from the supplied miniature or a safe imagined event. Say the message, draw or write it with support, then read it back. Choose one helpful edit together and explain what it improves.
adjust: Starter: arrange known word cards and add a full-stop card. Core: contribute a short sentence and one edit. Stretch: explain a meaning repair as well as a sentence-boundary or CVC-spelling check.
safety: Adult: read and model when needed. Accept speech, sign, AAC, pointing or a drawing with explanation. Use short turns. A page answer does not prove an actual conversation, reading performance or physical action.
tricky: “the dog ran.” already has a full stop. What could improve its beginning?
Change the first t to capital T: “The dog ran.” Keep the full stop.
The complete telling sentence “I can hop” has no ending mark. What can we add?
A full stop: “I can hop.” I is already a capital.
Does “My seed grew.” give us an initial short-vowel word with one letter for each of three sounds?

No. Use cat for this initial single-letter, short-vowel model. Seed has three sounds, /s/ /ee/ /d/, but ee is a two-letter vowel spelling. Grew has a /g/ /r/ start and the vowel spelling ew. Teach those patterns separately rather than treating them like cat.
faq: Should every correction happen at once?
No. Keep the child’s intended message, then choose one useful check at a time.
Can an adult scribe?
Yes. The child can contribute the idea, words, sound–letter choices or editing decisions. Record support honestly rather than claiming independent writing.
